CWE-174.name: Double Decoding of the Same Data
CWE-174.question: Does this function decode the same data twice, so a security check done between or before the decodes can be bypassed by double encoding?

any: a value is URL-, HTML- or base64-decoded and then decoded again before use
input is checked for dangerous characters such as ../ or < after one decode and then decoded again
javascript: decodeURIComponent applied to a value the framework has already decoded, such as req.query or req.params
python: unquote(unquote(x)), or unquote applied to a value from request.args, which is already decoded

any: data is decoded exactly once into canonical form before any validation
validation runs after the final decode and nothing decodes the value afterwards

distinguish_from.CWE-180: the order of validating and canonicalising is wrong but no second decode occurs
distinguish_from.CWE-675: the repeated operation is something other than decoding

CWE-188.name: Reliance on Data/Memory Layout
CWE-188.question: Does this function rely on how data is laid out in memory or in a binary message, such as member offsets, padding, variable adjacency or type punning?

any: a whole structure is copied to or from a byte buffer, file or socket with memcpy, fread, fwrite or send and the other side is assumed to share its layout
pointer arithmetic steps from one variable or member to a neighbouring one, assuming it sits next in memory
hard-coded offsets index into a structure or binary record instead of naming the fields
python: ctypes Structure or native struct formats map binary data assuming the platform's padding and alignment
javascript: fixed byte offsets into an ArrayBuffer assume a layout produced by C code on a particular machine
rust: transmute or pointer casts between types without #[repr(C)] or #[repr(packed)], or reliance on field order of a default-repr struct

any: each field is serialised and parsed individually with explicit sizes and byte order
offsets are computed with offsetof or sizeof, or the format is defined by a schema or serialisation library
rust: a serialisation crate or explicit from_le_bytes style parsing handles the format

distinguish_from.CWE-198: the only layout problem is the byte order of numeric fields
distinguish_from.REL-149: the layout dependence comes from writing one union member and reading another
distinguish_from.REL-180: the code reaches into or copies a FILE object

CWE-198.name: Use of Incorrect Byte Ordering
CWE-198.question: Does this function take multi-byte numbers from a file, network or device and use them without converting from the data's byte order?

any: an integer or float is read from a received buffer by pointer cast, memcpy or a bulk read and used directly with no byte-order conversion
numbers are assembled from bytes in an order that contradicts the protocol, for example little-endian shifts for a network-order field
c: a port, length or address field from a socket buffer is used without ntohs, ntohl or a be/le conversion helper, or a value is sent without htons/htonl
cpp: reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*> or istream::read into an integer from network or file bytes, with no byte-order conversion
python: int.from_bytes or struct.unpack is called with the wrong byte order or with native '@' order for wire data
javascript: DataView getUint16/getUint32 is called without the littleEndian argument matching the format, or a Uint32Array is laid over received bytes
rust: from_ne_bytes or a pointer cast is used on received bytes instead of from_be_bytes or from_le_bytes

any: every multi-byte field is converted with an explicit big- or little-endian decode that matches the format
the data is single bytes or text, so byte order does not apply
a parsing or serialisation library with a defined wire format does the decoding
cpp: std::byteswap with a std::endian check, or explicit shifts in the format's byte order

distinguish_from.CWE-188: the problem is padding, field offsets or overall layout rather than byte order
distinguish_from.CWE-1102: the issue is another machine-dependent representation such as type width or float encoding

CWE-242.name: Use of Inherently Dangerous Function
CWE-242.question: Does this function call a C or C++ function, such as gets, that has no way to be used safely whatever the arguments?

c: gets is called, which reads a line with no way to pass the destination size
operator >> reads into a plain char array through an istream with no width set
a similar unbounded input routine is used whose interface accepts no length
input is read with fgets, getline, std::getline or std::string, which take or manage a length
operator >> reads into std::string, or setw limits the width before reading into a char array
the dangerous name appears only in a comment, string or macro that redirects to a safe function

distinguish_from.CWE-676: the called function, such as strcpy or memcpy, can be safe when given correct sizes

CWE-253.name: Incorrect Check of Function Return Value
CWE-253.question: Does this function check a call's return value against the wrong value or in the wrong way, so errors are missed or success is seen as failure?

any: the error result is tested with the wrong comparison, such as < 0 for a function that signals failure with NULL or 0
c: malloc or fopen tested < 0, read or recv tested only == 0, or strcmp used directly as a true/false equality test
a size_t or unsigned return compared < 0, so an error value of -1 is never seen
cpp: if (s.find(x)) or s.find(x) >= 0 used to test for a match, where std::string::npos is the failure value and 0 a valid position
javascript: if (s.indexOf(x)) or if (!s.indexOf(x)), treating index 0 and -1 the wrong way round
python: if s.find(x): treating -1 as truthy and index 0 as false
rust: a Result checked with is_ok() while the success value is taken from a different call or ignored

any: the test matches the documented failure value of that exact function
an exception or Result is used and handled instead of a sentinel
cpp: find results are compared with npos, and a std::error_code is tested through its bool conversion
javascript: indexOf compared explicitly with -1, or includes() used

distinguish_from.CWE-252: the return value is not checked at all
distinguish_from.CWE-394: the code tests for the right sentinel but the callee can return a status the check does not expect

CWE-358.name: Improperly Implemented Security Check for Standard
CWE-358.question: Does this function implement a standard security protocol or check, such as TLS, JWT, OAuth or signature verification, but skip or weaken a step the standard requires?

any: a certificate is accepted without checking hostname, validity dates or chain to a trusted root
a token is accepted without checking signature, algorithm, expiry, issuer or audience
a nonce, state, MAC or padding check that the protocol mandates is missing or compares only part of the value
javascript: jwt.decode used instead of jwt.verify, or verify called with algorithms including 'none' or no algorithm list
python: jwt.decode with verify_signature False, or ssl contexts with check_hostname False

any: the function delegates to a maintained library call that performs all required checks with secure defaults
every mandated check is present and failure stops the operation

distinguish_from.CWE-295: the missing step is certificate validation in general and the more precise entry fits
distinguish_from.CWE-347: the missing step is verifying a cryptographic signature

CWE-393.name: Return of Wrong Status Code
CWE-393.question: Does this function return a status or result code that misstates what happened, such as success after an error or the wrong error code?

any: an error branch returns 0, true, OK or HTTP 200 although the operation failed
a caught exception is swallowed and the function returns a success value
the code returned does not match the failure, such as not-found for a permission error or a generic code that callers treat as success
each path returns a status that matches its actual outcome
errors are propagated by exception, Result or the callee's own code without change

distinguish_from.CWE-252: the function ignores a callee's status rather than returning a wrong one of its own
distinguish_from.CWE-636: the wrong success value grants access or weakens security on failure

CWE-424.name: Improper Protection of Alternate Path
CWE-424.question: Does this function provide a second route to protected functionality or data, such as an alternate endpoint, legacy flag or internal call, that skips the checks the main route applies?

any: a branch, parameter or alternate handler reaches the same protected action without the authentication or authorisation the normal path performs
an internal, legacy, API or export variant of an operation omits a validation present in the primary version
a direct file or object path serves content that is otherwise protected by a controller check
all branches go through the same check before the protected action
the check is enforced centrally, such as middleware or a decorator applied to every route involved

distinguish_from.CWE-288: the alternate path specifically bypasses authentication
distinguish_from.CWE-638: the check exists on the path but uses a stale earlier result

CWE-440.name: Expected Behavior Violation
CWE-440.question: Does this function fail to behave as its interface or the specification it implements requires, for example ignoring a documented parameter or contract?

any: a documented parameter, option or flag is accepted but ignored or has a different effect
an overridden or interface method breaks the contract of the base, such as an equals that is not symmetric or a comparator that is not consistent
the function implements a named standard or protocol operation but returns or handles results differently from it
the implementation honours each parameter and documented guarantee
no specification or contract is visible to compare against

distinguish_from.CWE-393: the only deviation is a wrong status code
distinguish_from.CWE-358: the deviation is a missing security check required by a standard

CWE-446.name: UI Discrepancy for Security Feature
CWE-446.question: Does this function show or report a security feature as enabled or saved when the setting was not actually applied?

any: a confirmation, toggle state or status message for a security setting is set before or regardless of whether applying it succeeded
an error from applying a security setting is ignored while the interface still reports success
the displayed security state is read from a local variable rather than the setting actually in force
the interface state is updated only after the setting is applied and confirmed
failures to apply are shown to the user

distinguish_from.CWE-447: the security feature has no implementation at all behind the control
distinguish_from.CWE-449: the control performs a different action from the one chosen
distinguish_from.CWE-448: the feature is obsolete and the user is not warned

CWE-447.name: Unimplemented or Unsupported Feature in UI
CWE-447.question: Does this function present or accept a security option, such as a toggle, setting or handler, that reports success but does not actually implement the protection?

any: a handler for a security setting stores or acknowledges the choice but nothing reads or applies it
a stub, TODO or empty body behind a security option that still returns success or shows a confirmation
a UI control for encryption, two-factor, privacy or locking that updates only the display state
the setting flows into code that enforces it
an unsupported option is disabled, hidden or reports an error

distinguish_from.CWE-446: the feature is implemented but the interface shows the wrong state
distinguish_from.CWE-449: the interface triggers a different action from the one requested

CWE-448.name: Obsolete Feature in UI
CWE-448.question: Does this function keep offering a deprecated or obsolete user-facing feature, such as an old option or command, without warning the user?

any: a menu item, option, command or flag marked deprecated in comments or code still runs with no warning shown
a legacy setting is accepted silently although it no longer has any effect or has a weaker replacement
using the deprecated feature produces a visible warning or deprecation notice
the obsolete option has been removed or disabled

distinguish_from.CWE-477: the code calls an obsolete function internally rather than exposing an obsolete feature to users
distinguish_from.CWE-447: the feature appears to work but was never implemented

CWE-449.name: The UI Performs the Wrong Action
CWE-449.question: Does this interface handler carry out a different action from the one the user selected, for example through a mis-wired button or swapped condition?

any: an event handler for one control calls the routine for a different action, such as a cancel button that confirms
a condition or mapping from user choice to action is inverted or uses the wrong key
the action is applied to a different item, scope or account from the one selected
tsx: onClick or onChange props wired to the wrong handler, or a handler closing over the wrong item in a mapped list

any: each control's handler performs exactly its labelled action on the selected target
the function is not an interface handler and has no user-selected action

distinguish_from.CWE-446: the right action runs but the interface reports the security state wrongly

CWE-451.name: User Interface (UI) Misrepresentation of Critical Information
CWE-451.question: Does this function display critical information, such as a URL, sender, file name or permission prompt, in a way that can hide or spoof its true value or source?

any: an untrusted display name, link text or title is shown in place of the real URL, address or origin
text from input is shown without stripping right-to-left overrides, control characters or excessive length that hide the real ending
security prompts or warnings can be overlaid, truncated or styled by untrusted content
javascript: link text from user data rendered with a different href, or window.open to untrusted content without showing its origin

any: the real origin or full value is shown and cannot be controlled by untrusted input
untrusted strings are sanitised of control and bidirectional characters before display

distinguish_from.CWE-1007: the spoofing relies specifically on look-alike characters
distinguish_from.CWE-79: untrusted content is injected as script or markup

CWE-474.name: Use of Function with Inconsistent Implementations
CWE-474.question: Does this function call a library function whose behaviour differs across operating systems or versions, relying on one platform's behaviour without guarding for others?

c: signal() whose handler reset semantics vary, strerror_r whose GNU and XSI forms differ, or _snprintf on Windows, which may not terminate
realpath, vfork, readdir_r or similar used assuming one platform's semantics
javascript: Date parsing of non-ISO strings, or locale-sensitive toLocaleString output parsed back as data
python: time.strftime with platform-only codes such as %-d, os.rename expected to overwrite on every OS, or select on non-socket handles
rust: std::fs::rename or file locking expected to behave identically on Windows and Unix

any: the function uses a portable alternative with uniform behaviour, such as sigaction, ISO 8601 parsing or os.replace
platform differences are handled by explicit conditional code

distinguish_from.CWE-589: the function does not exist at all on some target platforms rather than behaving differently

CWE-475.name: Undefined Behavior for Input to API
CWE-475.question: Does this function pass an argument to a library call for which the call's behaviour is undefined, such as overlapping buffers, NULL or an out-of-domain value?

c: memcpy, strcpy, strcat or sprintf with source and destination that may overlap
a NULL pointer passed to strlen, strcmp, printf %s or memcpy with a non-zero size
isalpha, toupper and other ctype functions given a plain char that may be negative
cpp: std::copy into a destination that starts inside the source range, or std::memcpy on objects that are not trivially copyable
std::sort or std::set given a comparator that is not a strict weak ordering, such as <=
memset, memcmp or strcmp applied to objects of a class with virtual functions or non-trivial members
javascript: sort given a comparator that is inconsistent or returns a boolean, giving engine-dependent results
python: a list or dict being mutated while the same object is iterated by a library call such as sorted, or a key function with side effects
rust: unsafe calls such as ptr::copy_nonoverlapping, from_raw_parts or str::from_utf8_unchecked given arguments that break their safety contract

any: the arguments are checked or constructed to meet every documented precondition of the call
c: memmove is used for possibly overlapping regions, and ctype arguments are cast to unsigned char
cpp: std::copy_backward or std::memmove handles overlapping ranges, and class types are copied by assignment or std::copy
python: Python library calls given bad input raise an exception rather than behaving unpredictably
rust: only safe Rust APIs are used, whose misuse panics or returns an error rather than being undefined

distinguish_from.REL-148: the undefined call is specifically a copy between overlapping regions
distinguish_from.REL-036: the argument is a numeric value outside a maths or library function's accepted range

CWE-476.name: NULL Pointer Dereference
CWE-476.question: Can this function dereference a pointer or reference that may be null at that point?

any: a value that the function itself shows may be null (a lookup result, an optional field, a pointer tested for null elsewhere in the function) is used before or without a null test on that path
c: the result of malloc, calloc, realloc, fopen, getenv, strchr or a similar call that can return NULL is dereferenced without a NULL test
a pointer is tested for NULL after it has already been dereferenced
cpp: a dynamic_cast<T*> result, weak_ptr::lock() result or moved-from std::unique_ptr is dereferenced without a null test
std::string or std::string_view constructed from a pointer that can be null, such as getenv's result
javascript: a property is read from a value that can be null or undefined, such as a find() or getElementById() result, without a check or optional chaining
python: an attribute or item is taken from a value that can be None, such as re.match() or dict.get() results, without a check
rust: a raw pointer from FFI or ptr::null is dereferenced inside unsafe without an is_null check

any: the pointer is tested for null on every path before each use
the value comes from a source that cannot be null, such as the address of a local or a constructor that throws on failure
the only possible null would come from a caller passing one, and nothing in this function suggests callers do
c: the allocation goes through a wrapper that aborts on failure
cpp: the pointer comes from new without std::nothrow, which throws std::bad_alloc rather than returning null, or a dynamic_cast to a reference, which throws
javascript: optional chaining (?.) or a nullish default (??) guards the access
rust: the value is a reference, Box or Option handled by match, if let, ? or unwrap_or, which cannot dereference null

distinguish_from.CWE-690: the null comes specifically from an unchecked return value and that is the more precise finding
distinguish_from.CWE-416: the pointer is not null but refers to memory that was already freed

CWE-477.name: Use of Obsolete Function
CWE-477.question: Does this function call a function or API that is deprecated or obsolete and has a safer or better-supported replacement?

c: gets, tmpnam, mktemp, asctime, ctime, or other functions removed or deprecated by the C standard or POSIX
cpp: std::auto_ptr, std::random_shuffle, std::bind1st, std::ptr_fun or std::strstream is used
javascript: new Buffer(...), escape/unescape, String.prototype.substr, document.write, or synchronous XMLHttpRequest
python: modules or calls removed or deprecated in Python 3, such as imp, asyncore, distutils, ssl.wrap_socket or os.popen2
rust: std::mem::uninitialized, the try! macro, or items marked #[deprecated] in std

any: only current, supported APIs are called
the name merely resembles a deprecated function but is a local or project-defined helper
c: the modern replacement is used, such as fgets, mkstemp or strftime
cpp: the modern replacement is used, such as std::unique_ptr, std::shuffle, a lambda or std::stringstream

distinguish_from.CWE-676: the function is current but inherently dangerous, such as strcpy, rather than obsolete
distinguish_from.CWE-242: the call can never be used safely, such as gets, and that is the more precise finding

CWE-484.name: Omitted Break Statement in Switch
CWE-484.question: Does a switch case in this function omit break so execution unintentionally runs on into the next case?

any: a case with its own statements ends without break, return, throw, continue or goto and the next case has different statements
the following case undoes or overwrites what the previous case just set, showing the run-on is unintended
every non-empty case ends with break, return, throw, continue or goto
empty case labels are stacked to share one body, which is a normal idiom
the run-on is marked deliberate with [[fallthrough]], __attribute__((fallthrough)) or a fall-through comment
python: Python match and if/elif chains never run on into the next branch
rust: Rust match arms never run on into the next arm

distinguish_from.REL-127: the run-on is marked deliberate yet still lacks an unconditional exit, which the coding-rule entry covers

CWE-489.name: Active Debug Code
CWE-489.question: Does this function contain debug, test or diagnostic code that stays active in normal builds, such as a backdoor flag, verbose dump or test bypass?

any: a debug or test flag, environment variable or magic parameter enables extra behaviour such as skipping checks or exposing internals
diagnostic dumps of internal state, stack traces or secrets on a path reachable in production
test-only endpoints, routes or commands that are not excluded from release builds
python: app.run(debug=True), DEBUG = True set in code, or pdb.set_trace() / breakpoint() left in
javascript: a debugger statement, or a route or handler marked for testing that is always registered

any: the debug path is compiled out or disabled in release builds, for example inside #ifndef NDEBUG or #[cfg(debug_assertions)]
ordinary logging at a configurable level that reveals nothing sensitive
the function is itself test code in a test file

distinguish_from.CWE-215: the debug code leaks sensitive information and that disclosure is the main finding
distinguish_from.CWE-912: the extra behaviour is a deliberately hidden feature rather than leftover debugging

CWE-506.name: Embedded Malicious Code
CWE-506.question: Does this function contain code that deliberately does harm, such as a hidden backdoor, data theft, destructive action or timed trigger, unrelated to its stated purpose?

any: obfuscated code, encoded strings or dynamic eval that decode to commands, URLs or payloads
sending credentials, environment variables, files or keystrokes to a hard-coded remote address
destructive actions such as deleting files or corrupting data triggered by a date, counter or hidden input
every action, including any network call, matches the function's evident purpose
obfuscation is only minified or generated code with a plain-source origin

distinguish_from.CWE-510: the malicious part is specifically a secret access route
distinguish_from.CWE-511: the malicious part is specifically a time or logic trigger
distinguish_from.CWE-512: the malicious part is specifically collecting user data covertly

CWE-507.name: Trojan Horse
CWE-507.question: Does this function appear to do one legitimate job while also covertly performing a harmful action the user would not expect?

any: a function named for a benign task, such as an update check or formatter, also downloads or runs remote code
an ordinary routine also copies secrets, files or tokens to an external address
harmful side effects are tucked into a helper whose name suggests something harmless
all side effects are consistent with the function's name and documented role
network or file activity is plainly part of the advertised feature

distinguish_from.CWE-509: the hidden code also tries to spread to other systems
distinguish_from.CWE-510: the covert extra is a secret access path into the system

CWE-508.name: Non-Replicating Malicious Code
CWE-508.question: Does this function carry out a hidden harmful action on the local system only, such as deleting data or installing persistence, without trying to spread?

any: covert deletion, encryption or corruption of local files or data not related to the function's purpose
silent installation of start-up entries, scheduled tasks, services or modified system files
file and system changes are part of the function's stated job and visible to the user
the code is an installer or maintenance routine doing what it documents

distinguish_from.CWE-509: the code also copies itself or attacks other machines

CWE-509.name: Replicating Malicious Code (Virus or Worm)
CWE-509.question: Does this function try to copy itself or its payload to other files, hosts or devices, such as scanning a network and pushing code to it?

any: scanning address ranges or contacts and then sending or executing a payload on discovered hosts
writing the program's own code into other executables, scripts, packages or removable drives
using stolen credentials or exploits to run the same code remotely
network or file distribution is a documented deployment or update feature with user consent
no code copies or runs the program elsewhere

distinguish_from.CWE-508: the harmful code stays on the local system

CWE-510.name: Trapdoor
CWE-510.question: Does this function contain a secret way in, such as a hard-coded master password, magic token or hidden command, that bypasses normal authentication or authorisation?

any: a login or permission check that also succeeds for a fixed username, password, token or header value
a hidden parameter or command that grants admin rights or skips checks
a listening socket or route that executes commands without authentication and is not part of any documented feature
authentication and authorisation have no special-case values
an emergency or service access path is documented, configurable and authenticated

distinguish_from.CWE-798: the fixed credential is used to connect to another system rather than to let someone in
distinguish_from.CWE-489: the bypass is a leftover debug or test switch

CWE-511.name: Logic/Time Bomb
CWE-511.question: Does this function trigger a harmful action when a hidden condition is met, such as a particular date, count, absence of a user or other trigger?

any: a date or time comparison that, once passed, deletes data, disables features or corrupts output
a counter, usage limit or check for a specific user or file that leads to destructive or disabling behaviour
a condition with no business meaning that guards damaging code
time or count conditions implement documented features such as expiry, licensing notices or retention policies
the conditioned action is harmless and visible to the user

distinguish_from.CWE-510: the hidden condition grants access rather than causing harm

CWE-512.name: Spyware
CWE-512.question: Does this function quietly collect personal data or user activity, such as keystrokes, contacts, location or browsing, and store or send it without the user's consent?

any: reading contacts, location, clipboard, keystrokes, screenshots or browser history with no consent check
sending collected user data to a remote endpoint unrelated to the feature the user is using
tracking or fingerprinting code that runs regardless of user preference
collection is gated on an explicit consent or permission check
the data is used only for the feature the user directly asked for

distinguish_from.CWE-359: private data is exposed to an unauthorised party rather than covertly gathered
distinguish_from.CWE-507: the hidden harm is something other than collecting user data

CWE-546.name: Suspicious Comment
CWE-546.question: Does a comment in this function say that the code is buggy, unfinished, insecure or a temporary hack?

any: a comment containing TODO, FIXME, XXX, HACK, BUG or LATER describes missing checks, missing error handling or known wrong behaviour
a comment admits a shortcut such as 'temporary', 'not thread safe', 'remove before release' or 'skip validation for now'
comments only explain what the code does or why, with no admission of defects or unfinished work
a TODO is purely about style, naming or a future feature unrelated to correctness or security
words like 'bug' or 'hack' appear only in identifiers, strings or links to resolved tickets

distinguish_from.CWE-1116: the comment is simply wrong about what the code does rather than flagging a known problem

CWE-547.name: Use of Hard-coded, Security-relevant Constants
CWE-547.question: Does this function use bare numeric or string literals for security-relevant values instead of named constants?

any: key lengths, iteration counts, permission masks, token lifetimes, retry limits or buffer limits for security checks are written as raw numbers
the same security-relevant literal appears several times in the function, so changing the policy means finding each copy
c: calls such as chmod(path, 0777), umask(0) or a key size passed as 16 or 32 written inline
python: os.chmod(path, 0o777), hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac with an inline iteration count, or timeouts as bare numbers

any: the values come from named constants, enums, configuration or a policy object
the literal is not security relevant, such as a loop index start, an array index of 0 or 1, or a display width

distinguish_from.CWE-798: the hard-coded value is a password, key or other credential rather than a policy number

CWE-560.name: Use of umask() with chmod-style Argument
CWE-560.question: Does this function call umask with a value written as if it were a chmod permission mode, such as 0644 or 0755?

c: umask(0644), umask(0755), umask(0600) or similar, where the value lists the permissions to grant rather than to remove
a variable holding a desired file mode is passed straight to umask
umask is given a mask of bits to remove, such as 022, 027 or 077
the mode value is passed to chmod, open or mkdir rather than umask

distinguish_from.CWE-732: the permissions are wrong for another reason, not because of an inverted umask value

CWE-561.name: Dead Code
CWE-561.question: Does this function contain code that no execution path can reach?

any: statements after an unconditional return, break, continue, throw or goto in the same block
a branch guarded by a condition that is always false given the function's own code, such as testing an unsigned value for < 0
code after a call that never returns, such as exit, abort or panic, in the same path
python: statements after return or raise in the same block
rust: statements after a diverging expression such as return, panic!, unreachable! or loop without break

any: every block can be reached under some input or state
the guarded code depends on a configuration constant, build flag or platform check that can be true in other builds
a defensive default case or assertion is placed for robustness

distinguish_from.REL-042: for C and C++ code, the more precise rule on statements that can never be executed
distinguish_from.CWE-570: the root cause is an expression that always evaluates to false
distinguish_from.CWE-563: the code runs but its stored value is never used

CWE-562.name: Return of Stack Variable Address
CWE-562.question: Does this function return a pointer or reference to one of its own local variables or arrays, which no longer exist once it returns?

c: return &local; or return of a local array name, or of a pointer into a local buffer
a pointer variable set to a local's address and then returned
cpp: returning a reference or string_view to a local object, or c_str() or data() of a local std::string

c: the returned storage is static, heap-allocated or supplied by the caller
the value is returned by copy rather than by address

distinguish_from.REL-145: the local's address escapes through a global, an out-parameter or a stored structure rather than the return value
distinguish_from.CWE-416: the dangling pointer refers to heap memory that was freed

CWE-563.name: Assignment to Variable without Use
CWE-563.question: Does this function assign a value to a variable that is then overwritten or goes out of scope without being read?

any: a variable is assigned and then assigned again before any read on that path
a return value or computed result is stored in a local that is never used afterwards
an error code is captured into a variable but never checked
every assigned value is read on at least one later path
the variable is an initial default that is read when a later branch does not overwrite it
the store is to a field, global, volatile object or reference visible outside the function
python: the name is _ or another explicit throwaway
rust: the variable is named with a leading underscore or let _ =, marking it as deliberately unused

distinguish_from.REL-043: an operation runs with no effect without assigning to a variable
distinguish_from.CWE-252: a function's return value is ignored entirely rather than stored and left unused

CWE-570.name: Expression is Always False
CWE-570.question: Does this function contain a condition or expression that can never be true, so the code it guards never runs?

any: a comparison impossible for the type, such as an unsigned value tested < 0 or a char compared with a value outside its range

CWE-1071.question: Does this function contain an empty code block, such as an if, else, loop or function body with no statements?

any: an if, else, while or for body consists of {} or only a lone semicolon
a stray semicolon right after if (...) or for (...) makes the intended body run unconditionally
python: a block contains only pass or ... where work was clearly expected

any: the empty block has a comment explaining that doing nothing is intended
the empty loop is a deliberate busy-wait or the loop header does all the work, as in while (*p++) ;
the empty body is a required default implementation, such as an abstract or no-op hook

distinguish_from.CWE-1069: the empty block is an exception handler such as catch or except

CWE-1075.name: Unconditional Control Flow Transfer outside of Switch Block
CWE-1075.question: Does this function transfer control unconditionally with goto, or an equivalent jump, outside of a switch statement?

any: a goto statement appears outside a switch, jumping to a label elsewhere in the function
c: setjmp and longjmp are used to jump across normal control flow
javascript: a labelled break or continue jumps out of several nested blocks to an outer label

any: control flow uses only if, loops, return, plain break and continue, and exceptions
python: the language has no goto; break, continue and return are structured
rust: the language has no goto; labelled break and continue on loops are structured

distinguish_from.REL-118: a C or C++ goto is used and the more precise rule is the one about goto
distinguish_from.CWE-1119: the concern is the large number of unconditional branches rather than any single one

CWE-1076.name: Insufficient Adherence to Expected Conventions
CWE-1076.question: Does the function break common coding conventions, such as style rules, misleading comments, heavy global state, preprocessor misuse or missing C++ copy and destructor rules?

any: comments that are misleading, suspicious (TODO, FIXME, HACK) or that disable code, or confusing literals and identifiers
the function relies on many global or module-level variables
hard-coded security-relevant numbers appear where named constants would be expected
c: #include, #define or #undef lines placed inside the function body
cpp: a class with pointer members or virtual methods is copied or deleted through a base pointer in the function

any: the function is short, uses only locals and parameters, and has accurate or no comments

CWE-1078.name: Inappropriate Source Code Style or Formatting
CWE-1078.question: Does the function's source show style problems, such as suspicious or inaccurate comments, confusing literals, inconsistent names or magic security constants?

any: comments containing TODO, FIXME, HACK or BUG, or comments that contradict the code beside them
hard-coded numbers for security values such as key sizes, permissions or timeouts
names in the function that follow mixed conventions or differ only by case or underscores
c: octal literals with a leading zero, a lowercase l suffix, nested /* in comments or a // comment ending in a backslash

any: consistent naming, accurate comments and named constants throughout the function

CWE-1079.name: Parent Class without Virtual Destructor Method
CWE-1079.reason: Whether a base class with subclasses lacks a virtual destructor is decided by the class declarations, which no single function body contains.

CWE-1087.name: Class with Virtual Method without a Virtual Destructor
CWE-1087.reason: Whether a class with virtual methods also declares a virtual destructor is a property of the class declaration, not of any one function body.

CWE-1093.name: Excessively Complex Data Representation
CWE-1093.question: Does this function build or traverse data through an unnecessarily convoluted structure, such as deeply nested containers or parallel arrays kept in sync by hand?

any: values are kept in parallel arrays or lists indexed together instead of one record type
data is accessed through several levels of nested maps, lists or pointers, such as a[x][y]["k"][i] or p->a->b->c->d
the same information is stored in two or more forms that the function must keep consistent
the function uses simple records or classes whose shape matches the data
nesting reflects a real external format, such as parsed JSON, and is accessed in one clear place

distinguish_from.CWE-1120: the complexity is in control flow, branching or length rather than in data representation

CWE-1095.name: Loop Condition Value Update within the Loop
CWE-1095.question: Does the function contain a loop whose controlling variable or condition is changed inside the loop body?

any: a for loop counter is assigned or incremented inside the body as well as in the loop header
a while or for condition tests a value, such as a length or end pointer, that the body modifies
every loop changes its counter only in the header and the body does not touch the tested values

CWE-1098.name: Data Element containing Pointer Item without Proper Copy Control Element
CWE-1098.reason: Whether a type with pointer members defines copy and assignment control is set by the type's declaration, not by one function's code.

CWE-1099.name: Inconsistent Naming Conventions for Identifiers
CWE-1099.question: Do identifiers in the function follow inconsistent naming styles, or include names that are easily confused with each other?

any: locals and parameters mix styles such as camelCase, snake_case and Hungarian prefixes for similar things
two names in scope differ only by case, an underscore or look-alike characters such as l and 1 or O and 0
names in the function follow one style and are clearly distinct

CWE-1100.name: Insufficient Isolation of System-Dependent Functions
CWE-1100.question: Does this function mix operating system or platform-specific calls into general logic instead of calling an isolating wrapper?

any: platform-specific APIs, such as Win32, POSIX, RTOS or device driver calls, are called directly among business or algorithm logic
the body branches on the platform and has separate inline implementations for each
c: #ifdef _WIN32 or #ifdef __linux__ blocks inside the function choose between different system calls
python: checks on sys.platform or os.name select different subprocess commands or file paths inside the logic
javascript: process.platform checks or direct child_process shell commands specific to one OS are embedded in the logic
rust: cfg(target_os) blocks or platform crates such as libc or windows-sys are used directly inside general logic

any: the function is itself the platform wrapper whose only role is to adapt one system API
only portable standard library facilities are used

distinguish_from.CWE-1105: the machine dependence is assembly, data layout or hardware access rather than operating system calls

CWE-1102.name: Reliance on Machine-Dependent Data Representation
CWE-1102.question: Does this function's result depend on how the machine represents data, such as type sizes, signedness, byte order, padding or float format?

any: raw bytes of a multi-byte number or structure are reinterpreted, copied or sent as if every machine used the same layout
code assumes a particular type width or signedness, for example storing a pointer or long in a 32-bit field or relying on plain char being signed
floating-point values are compared or serialised bit for bit as if their encoding were fixed
cpp: reinterpret_cast<char*> of an integer or struct is passed to ostream::write or istream::read for a file or socket format
python: struct.pack or struct.unpack uses native mode ('@' or no prefix) for data written to files or the network, or array/ctypes buffers are shared across machines
javascript: a DataView, Float32Array or Uint32Array view over an ArrayBuffer is read or written without stating byte order, then exchanged with another system
rust: transmute, to_ne_bytes or from_ne_bytes is used on data that leaves the process

any: values are encoded and decoded field by field with an explicit byte order and explicit fixed sizes
the data never leaves the process and only ordinary typed operations are applied to it
c: fixed-width types from stdint.h and sizeof are used wherever width matters, with hton/ntoh style conversions at boundaries
cpp: std::endian is checked and std::byteswap or explicit shifts convert std::uint32_t style fixed-width fields at boundaries
python: struct formats use an explicit '<', '>' or '!' prefix, or int.to_bytes/from_bytes give the byte order
rust: to_le_bytes, to_be_bytes or a serialisation crate with a defined format is used

distinguish_from.REL-031: the issue is just declaring a plain int, long or char where a fixed-width type was expected
distinguish_from.CWE-198: the issue is specifically a missing or wrong byte-order conversion of received data
distinguish_from.CWE-188: the code relies on padding, member offsets or the placement of variables in memory

CWE-1104.name: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components
CWE-1104.reason: Whether a third-party component is still maintained is a fact about its upstream project, not visible in a function's source.

CWE-1105.name: Insufficient Encapsulation of Machine-Dependent Functionality
CWE-1105.question: Does the function use processor, compiler or platform-specific features such as inline assembly, raw memory layout, byte order or hardware registers directly in its logic?

any: inline assembly, compiler intrinsics or vendor extensions appear inside the function
the code depends on structure layout, padding, byte order or raw reinterpretation of memory
hardware registers, fixed addresses or platform-specific system calls are accessed directly
c: asm, __asm__, unions or pointer casts used to view the same bytes as different types, or direct access to FILE internals
python: ctypes, struct in native mode or platform checks such as sys.platform drive the logic
javascript: typed arrays or DataView over shared binary buffers, or checks on process.platform or navigator.platform
rust: asm!, transmute, #[repr] layout assumptions or cfg(target_arch) branches inside the logic

any: the function uses only ordinary portable language operations and library calls with no binary data or platform checks
machine-specific work is done only by calling a named wrapper whose body is elsewhere

CWE-1108.name: Excessive Reliance on Global Variables
CWE-1108.question: Does this function depend on reading or setting several global or module-level variables instead of using parameters, return values or object state?

any: the function reads or writes several global or file-scope variables to receive inputs or pass back results
the function's behaviour changes according to mutable global flags set elsewhere
python: global or nonlocal statements are used to change module-level state
javascript: the function assigns to module-level let variables, window or globalThis properties to share state
rust: static mut variables, or global Mutex or lazy statics, carry state between calls

any: the function uses only parameters, locals, its own object's fields and return values
the only module-level names used are constants, imported functions or a logger
a single global such as a hardware register block or singleton is accessed through a clear interface

distinguish_from.CWE-1126: a variable is declared in a wider scope within the function than its use requires

CWE-1113.name: Inappropriate Comment Style
CWE-1113.question: Does the function contain comments whose style could hide code or mislead, such as nested comment openers or line comments that continue onto the next line?

any: a block comment contains /* or // inside it
a // comment ends with a backslash, joining the next line into the comment
comment styles are mixed in a way that makes it hard to see where comments end
comments are simple, closed on the same or following lines, and contain no comment markers

CWE-1116.name: Inaccurate Source Code Comments
CWE-1116.question: Does a comment in this function describe behaviour, units, limits or conditions that the code next to it does not actually implement?

any: a comment states a value, unit, range or condition that differs from the code, such as 'timeout in ms' beside a value used as seconds, or 'max 10' beside a check for 16
a doc comment lists parameters, return values or exceptions that do not match the signature or the code paths
a comment says a case is handled, checked or locked when the code below does not do so
comments agree with the code they describe, or the function has no explanatory comments
the comment is vague but not contradicted by the code
the comment admits a known gap, which is a suspicious comment rather than an inaccurate one

distinguish_from.CWE-546: the comment admits a bug, hack or unfinished work rather than misdescribing the code

CWE-1119.name: Excessive Use of Unconditional Branching
CWE-1119.question: Does the function use goto or other unconditional jumps, such as backward jumps or jumps into blocks?

any: one or more goto statements, including goto cleanup or retry patterns
a goto to a label earlier in the function, or to a label inside another block
c: setjmp and longjmp used for control flow

any: the function has no goto, setjmp or longjmp

CWE-1120.name: Excessive Code Complexity
CWE-1120.question: Is this function excessively complex, with very many branches, deep nesting or tangled control flow that is hard to test fully?

any: many decision points (if, case, loop, &&, ||, catch) in one function, giving a high cyclomatic complexity
nesting four or more levels deep, or a single function that runs to hundreds of lines doing several jobs
control flow that jumps around with goto, labelled breaks, flags or early exits scattered through nested blocks
the function is short with a few shallow branches
length comes from a flat list of independent cases, such as a switch table or a data initialiser

distinguish_from.CWE-1075: the issue is specifically a goto or unconditional jump outside a switch
distinguish_from.CWE-1095: the issue is specifically a loop whose condition variable is changed inside the body
distinguish_from.CWE-1093: the complexity is in the shape of the data rather than in control flow

CWE-1123.name: Excessive Use of Self-Modifying Code
CWE-1123.question: Does this function change its own or other program code at run time, such as writing machine instructions or rewriting function definitions?

any: the function writes into memory that holds executable code, or patches instructions or jump targets
c: mprotect or VirtualProtect makes code pages writable or executable and bytes are then written to them
python: the function reassigns other functions, methods or __code__ attributes, or uses exec to generate replacement definitions
javascript: the function reassigns methods on its own module or prototype, or builds code text and runs it with eval or new Function
rust: unsafe code writes to a function pointer target or to memory mapped as executable

any: the function only selects behaviour through ordinary branches, function pointers, callbacks or strategy objects
code generation is a documented JIT or test mock confined to one module
rust: safe Rust code, which cannot write to executable memory

distinguish_from.CWE-95: the code passes untrusted input to eval or a similar interpreter

CWE-1126.name: Declaration of Variable with Unnecessarily Wide Scope
CWE-1126.question: Does this function declare a variable in a wider scope than needed, for example at the top of the function when it is used only inside one inner block or loop?

any: a variable declared at function scope is used only within one loop, branch or nested block
a loop counter or temporary is declared outside the loop and not used after it
c: the function uses a file-scope or global variable to hold a value that only this function needs within one call
javascript: var declares a variable whose use is confined to one block, where let or const in that block would do

any: every variable is used across the scope where it is declared, or its value is needed after the inner block
the variable is declared early because the language or coding standard requires it, such as C89 block-start declarations
python: Python has function-level scope only, so a variable first assigned inside a block is already as narrow as the language allows

distinguish_from.CWE-1108: the function relies on several shared global variables rather than one over-wide declaration

CWE-1164.name: Irrelevant Code
CWE-1164.question: Does this function contain code that does nothing useful, such as unreachable statements, values computed and discarded, empty blocks or commented-out code?

any: statements that can never run, or an assignment whose value is overwritten or never read
an expression statement whose result is discarded and which has no side effect, such as x == 1; or a + b;
an empty block, or code left in comments
every statement contributes to the result, state or side effects of the function
an apparently unused value is a deliberate (void) cast or placeholder for a required API
an empty block carries a comment explaining why nothing is done

distinguish_from.CWE-561: a specific statement or branch can never be reached
distinguish_from.CWE-563: a variable is assigned a value that is never read
distinguish_from.CWE-1071: a block such as an if body or loop body is empty

CWE-1177.name: Use of Prohibited Code
CWE-1177.question: Does this function call a function, API or library that common banned lists or coding standards prohibit for this language?

any: a call to a function that widely used banned lists forbid, where a safer replacement exists in the language or platform
c: gets, strcpy, strcat, sprintf, vsprintf, scanf with %s, strtok, tmpnam or mktemp is called
javascript: eval, new Function, setTimeout or setInterval with a string argument, or document.write is used
python: eval, exec, pickle.loads, marshal.loads, os.system or yaml.load without a safe loader is called
rust: std::mem::uninitialized, mem::zeroed for types where zero is invalid, or a deprecated unsafe std API is used

any: only bounded or safe replacements are used, such as snprintf, strlcpy, JSON.parse, ast.literal_eval or MaybeUninit
the name only matches a project wrapper that does its own bounds or input checks
the call appears only in a comment, string, test fixture or disabled code

distinguish_from.CWE-242: the call is to gets or another function that can never be used safely
distinguish_from.CWE-676: the function can be used safely and the question is whether this call site misuses it

CWE-1242.name: Inclusion of Undocumented Features or Chicken Bits
CWE-1242.reason: Concerns undocumented hardware configuration bits designed into a device, which function source code cannot show.

CWE-1277.name: Firmware Not Updateable
CWE-1277.reason: Whether firmware can be updated is a product capability, not something one function's source can show.

CWE-1329.name: Reliance on Component That is Not Updateable
CWE-1329.reason: Whether a component can be updated or patched depends on product packaging and deployment, not on one function's code.

CWE-1341.name: Multiple Releases of Same Resource or Handle
CWE-1341.question: Can this function release the same resource or handle twice, such as freeing memory or closing a file descriptor that was already released?

c: free, fclose, close or a destroy call on a pointer or descriptor that an earlier path already released and did not reset
pthread_join or thrd_join called twice on the same thread, or after it was detached
cpp: delete or delete[] is applied to a raw member pointer in two places, such as a destructor and a release method, without nulling it
two std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr objects are constructed from the same raw pointer
join() or detach() called on a std::thread that was already joined or detached, with no joinable() check
javascript: fs.closeSync or fs.close on the same fd twice, or a lock release called in both a catch and a finally block
python: os.close(fd) twice, or a lock released explicitly and then again by a context manager or finally
rust: Box::from_raw, libc::close or a manual drop on the same raw pointer or descriptor more than once inside unsafe
any: the release is done both in an error branch and again in shared cleanup code reached afterwards
the handle is set to NULL, -1 or None right after release and checked before any further release
each path releases the resource exactly once
cpp: a single std::unique_ptr, std::fstream or other RAII owner releases the resource once in its destructor
python: closing a Python file or socket object twice, which is a harmless no-op
rust: ownership with Drop releases the resource once and the compiler forbids a second use

distinguish_from.CWE-415: the double release is specifically freeing heap memory twice
distinguish_from.CWE-675: the repeated once-only operation is not a release

CWE-1357.name: Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component
CWE-1357.reason: Whether a component is trustworthy enough is a supply chain and design property that no single function's source can show.

CWE-1395.name: Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component
CWE-1395.reason: Known vulnerabilities in a dependency depend on its version and advisories, recorded in manifests rather than in a function's code.
